title: Ezekiel 28:11–19
context: The LORD’s word comes to the prophet with a command to take up a lamentation over the king of Tyre (28:11–12). The lament describes him as the seal of full measure, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty. He was in Eden, the garden of God, adorned with precious stones; he was the anointed cherub who covers, set on the holy mountain of God and walking among the stones of fire (28:12–14). He was perfect in his ways from the day he was created until unrighteousness was found in him. Through the abundance of his commerce he was filled with violence and sinned, and so he was cast out of God’s mountain, cast to the ground, and turned to ashes before all who watched (28:15–19). Readers have understood this king in several ways. Many take him as the historical ruler of Tyre, described through bold imagery drawn from Eden, the sanctuary, and ancient royal ideals; the references to commerce (28:16, 18) and to kings looking on (28:17) anchor the lament in Tyre’s history. Many read the imagery typologically, seeing the king cast in the role of a primal figure in Eden, so that his fall echoes the first human fall (compare Genesis 2–3). Many Christian readers, past and present, also see behind the king a portrait of the fall of Satan, often reading the passage alongside Isaiah 14:12–15. Some combine these readings, holding that the human king is the subject while the imagery reaches beyond him. Arminian and Reformed readers are found holding each of these views, and neither tradition requires or excludes any of them. The cherub, the stones, and the holy mountain are evocative images whose precise background is uncertain. Both traditions agree on the lament’s central lesson: one given splendor and wisdom fell through pride and violence, and the LORD judged him justly.

verses.text: Moreover the LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD’s word comes to the prophet once more, and a second message about Tyre’s ruler begins, this time a lament rather than an oracle of judgment. Arminian readers see the LORD returning to the same subject with a different form of speech, so that grief over what was lost accompanies the sentence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the shift from “the prince of Tyre” (28:2) to “the king of Tyre” (28:12); many take the titles as interchangeable, while some who see a figure behind the king find meaning in the change. Shared ground: both traditions read the word as coming from the LORD through the prophet, and both read the lament as closely tied to the oracle of verses 1–10.

verses.text: “Son of man, take up a lamentation over the king of Tyre, and tell him, ‘The Lord GOD says: “You were the seal of full measure, full of wisdom, and perfect in beauty.
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet, addressed as “son of man,” is told to “take up a lamentation over the king of Tyre.” The lament begins: “You were the seal of full measure, full of wisdom, and perfect in beauty.” Arminian readers hear language of extraordinary privilege, and they see the greatness of the gifts as the measure of the responsibility that came with them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers take “seal of full measure” as a picture of completeness, an image whose exact sense is uncertain but whose point is exalted standing. Shared ground: both traditions read the opening as describing gifts received rather than self-made, and both note that “perfect in beauty” echoes Tyre’s own boast in 27:3.

verses.text: You were in Eden, the garden of God. Every precious stone adorned you: ruby, topaz, emerald, chrysolite, onyx, jasper, sapphire, turquoise, and beryl. Gold work of tambourines and of pipes was in you. They were prepared in the day that you were created.
verses.arminianNotes: “You were in Eden, the garden of God.” Nine precious stones are named, with gold work, prepared “in the day that you were created.” Arminian readers who take the historical king as the subject see royal splendor described in the language of paradise; those who read typologically see him cast as a figure placed in Eden like the first human (compare Genesis 2:8, 15).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that all nine stones also appear on the high priest’s breastpiece (compare Exodus 28:17–20), suggesting priestly or sanctuary imagery to many readers. Those who hold the fall-of-Satan reading see Eden as pointing to the adversary who appeared there (compare Genesis 3:1; Revelation 12:9). Shared ground: both traditions hold that this splendor was given by God, not earned.

verses.text: You were the anointed cherub who covers. Then I set you up on the holy mountain of God. You have walked up and down in the middle of the stones of fire.
verses.arminianNotes: “You were the anointed cherub who covers. Then I set you up on the holy mountain of God.” He walked among “the stones of fire.” Arminian readers who read the passage of the historical king see his royal office pictured as a guardian figure in God’s presence; those reading typologically see a privileged figure placed near God, as Adam was.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the echo of the cherubim guarding Eden (Genesis 3:24) and covering the ark (Exodus 25:20); those who hold the fall-of-Satan reading see here an exalted angelic being. Shared ground: both traditions treat the holy mountain and the stones of fire as evocative images of uncertain background, and both hear in “I set you up” a nearness that the LORD himself granted.

verses.text: You were perfect in your ways from the day that you were created, until unrighteousness was found in you.
verses.arminianNotes: “You were perfect in your ways from the day that you were created, until unrighteousness was found in you.” Arminian readers emphasize that the fall was real and arose within the figure himself: one made good chose wrongly, and the sin was his own, not God’s.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise stress that the figure was made upright and that unrighteousness arose in him, not from God (compare Ecclesiastes 7:29), and they hold this within God’s governance of all things. Shared ground: whether they apply the verse to the king, to an Adamic figure, or to Satan, both traditions read it as saying that God made the creature good and that the guilt lies with the one who sinned.

verses.text: By the abundance of your commerce, your insides were filled with violence, and you have sinned. Therefore I have cast you as profane out of God’s mountain. I have destroyed you, covering cherub, from the middle of the stones of fire.
verses.arminianNotes: “By the abundance of your commerce, your insides were filled with violence, and you have sinned.” Therefore the LORD cast him “as profane out of God’s mountain.” Arminian readers see the mention of commerce as tying the lament closely to Tyre’s trade (compare 27:12–25), a strong anchor for those who read the figure as the historical king.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that some who hold the fall-of-Satan reading take “commerce” in a broader sense, while those who read typologically see an expulsion like Adam’s from Eden (Genesis 3:23–24). Shared ground: both traditions read greed and violence as the sin that brought the expulsion, and both see the LORD as the just judge who removes the profane from his holy presence.

verses.text: Your heart was lifted up because of your beauty. You have corrupted your wisdom by reason of your splendor. I have cast you to the ground. I have laid you before kings, that they may see you.
verses.arminianNotes: “Your heart was lifted up because of your beauty. You have corrupted your wisdom by reason of your splendor.” The LORD cast him to the ground before kings. Arminian readers see pride as the root of the fall, the same sin charged against the prince in 28:2, and they hear a warning that gifts can become the occasion of self-exaltation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this verse is one reason many Christian readers connect the passage with the devil’s fall through pride (compare 1 Timothy 3:6), while those who read it of the historical king see the watching kings as his fellow rulers. Shared ground: both traditions read pride as the heart of the sin and apply the lesson to every human heart, whatever reading they hold.

verses.text: By the multitude of your iniquities, in the unrighteousness of your commerce, you have profaned your sanctuaries. Therefore I have brought out a fire from the middle of you. It has devoured you. I have turned you to ashes on the earth in the sight of all those who see you.
verses.arminianNotes: “By the multitude of your iniquities, in the unrighteousness of your commerce, you have profaned your sanctuaries.” Fire comes out from the middle of him and turns him to ashes. Arminian readers see the sin as self-destructive, since the fire comes from within, and they read the judgment as the fruit of the figure’s own choices.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that it is the LORD who speaks: “I have brought out a fire,” executing just judgment, while the iniquities remain the figure’s own. Shared ground: both traditions read the mention of commerce and sanctuaries as linking the lament to Tyre’s history and worship, and both see the burning as a public judgment carried out in the sight of all.

verses.text: All those who know you among the peoples will be astonished at you. You have become a terror, and you will exist no more.” ’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: “All those who know you among the peoples will be astonished at you. You have become a terror, and you will exist no more.” The lament closes with a refrain much like 27:36. Arminian readers hear a sober warning for all who trust in splendor: the end of pride is ruin before watching eyes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the finality of the LORD’s judgment, and those who hold the fall-of-Satan reading often connect it with the final defeat of the adversary (compare Revelation 20:10). Shared ground: both traditions read the closing refrain as linking the king’s fall to the city’s fall in chapter 27, and both see the LORD’s justice displayed before the nations.
